stories.title: Google Search Falls Below Half of Alphabet's Revenue
stories.story:
For twenty-five years, Google Search was not merely a product — it was the entire financial logic of one of the most valuable companies on earth. This week, for the first time since Alphabet began reporting the figure separately, that logic cracked. In Q3 2026, Google Search brought in $63.4 billion — a record dollar amount — yet it amounted to only 49.7% of Alphabet's total revenue. The company's search share had never before dipped below 52.8%.

The mechanism is instructive: Search didn't shrink; everything else grew faster. Google Cloud more than doubled year-over-year, surging 103% to $30.7 billion, driven by enterprise demand for AI infrastructure. Search's slide from majority to minority happened in just two quarters, as Cloud's share jumped from 18% to 24% of total revenue.

But the more troubling signal is buried inside Search itself. Queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years — CEO Sundar Pichai said so on the earnings call — yet Search revenue grew only 12%, down sharply from 19% two quarters ago. The gap points to a structural monetization problem: AI Mode queries run roughly three times longer than classic searches but earn less per query. Google is cannibalizing its own ad yield with the very product it built to defend against ChatGPT.

Alphabet shares fell roughly 10% and the company posted its first top-and-bottom-line earnings miss in nearly four years. Free cash flow turned negative at -$9.07 billion, even as capex guidance for 2027 is set to rise significantly. The company is spending like Cloud is the future while quietly watching Search — the engine that paid for everything — begin its structural transition from a certainty to a bet.
stories.hook: Google has more searches than ever and is earning less from each one — that's not a bad quarter, that's a changed business.
stories.source: Alphabet Q3 2026 SEC Filing; CNBC; Kadoa Company Atlas

stories.title: Intel's AI Boom Is Cannibalizing Its Own PC Business
stories.story:
Intel reported a 78% surge in data center and AI revenue last quarter — and then watched its stock crater 29% in a single session, its worst single-day drop since the 1970s. The apparent paradox dissolves once you trace the mechanism.

AI data centers are the world's most voracious consumers of DRAM memory chips. That insatiable appetite has tightened global memory supply and pushed prices high enough that building a PC has become noticeably more expensive. Consumers are walking away. Intel's client computing division — the old reliable engine of the company — fell 5% year over year, and Intel now expects PC unit sales industry-wide to shrink roughly 12% in 2026 and 10% again in 2027. Q4 guidance came in $1.5 billion short of Wall Street's estimate, and adjusted earnings are forecast to fall from $0.52 to $0.25 per share in a single quarter.

The government has skin in this. The Trump administration led the U.S. into a 10% equity stake in Intel under the CHIPS Act framework; Friday's collapse wiped about $12 billion off that position. Nvidia, which also holds a stake, lost roughly $6 billion in paper value alongside it.

What Intel's earnings really reveal is a structural tension at the heart of the AI buildout. The hyperscalers — Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Google — are collectively responsible for more than a third of all capital expenditure in the S&P 500. Their spending is so enormous it is now distorting component markets downstream, crowding out the consumer electronics sector that once made semiconductors a mass-market business. The AI boom and the PC bust are not separate stories. They are the same story told from two ends of the supply chain.
stories.hook: The AI boom isn't just disrupting industries — it's disrupting the very supply chains that built it.

stories.title: North Korea Drained Binance in Twenty Minutes
stories.story:
On the evening of October 29, $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency began flowing out of Binance wallets across ten separate blockchains — Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, Tron, and six others. Most of it was gone in roughly twenty minutes. The attacker, according to blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis, was TraderTraitor: North Korea's elite state-sponsored hacking unit, the same group that carried out the $1.5 billion Bybit heist in February 2025. The Binance theft is four times larger — the biggest crypto theft ever recorded.

The mechanism matters. Investigators believe hackers compromised a Binance engineer's laptop to hijack the exchange's hot wallet signing infrastructure — the system that authorizes outgoing transactions. Once inside, they obtained transaction signatures in advance, a preparation technique consistent with earlier North Korean operations. Binance moved quickly to freeze roughly $3 billion in assets with blockchain partners, but an estimated $3.3 billion remained unfrozen and in motion through obfuscation networks.

Binance pledged to cover all losses through its emergency reserve fund — which holds only $1 billion, meaning the exchange itself may have to absorb several billion dollars in direct losses. Bitcoin barely moved on the news, a sign of how normalized state-level crypto theft has become. But the real test is structural: Pyongyang has now stolen enough cryptocurrency in two years to fund a mid-sized nation's military budget. The question is no longer whether crypto can be hacked at scale. It's whether centralized exchanges can survive being a sovereign adversary's primary revenue stream.
stories.hook: The world's largest crypto exchange just got robbed by a government, in twenty minutes, and the market shrugged.

stories.title: AI Search Is Eating Reddit From the Outside In
stories.story:
Reddit beat Wall Street on every number that is supposed to matter. In the third quarter of 2026, revenue grew 53% year-over-year, earnings per share came in at $1.40 against a $1.33 consensus, and advertising revenue climbed 54% to $847 million. Then the stock fell 29% in a single session — its worst day since its 2024 IPO.

The reason was a single data point buried in the earnings call: search referrals to Reddit had been declining by more than one million visits per week on average in October alone. CEO Steve Huffman named the cause plainly — AI-generated summaries from Google, which now answer questions directly in the search results page rather than directing users to the underlying source. Reddit had built much of its growth thesis on being the internet's most human answer to any question, the page Google's algorithm reliably surfaced. That surfacing is ending.

The mechanism is straightforward and brutal. Google's AI Overviews synthesize Reddit threads into a tidy paragraph. The user gets the answer. Reddit gets nothing — no click, no session, no ad impression. U.S. daily active users actually fell 2% from a year earlier to 50.7 million, even as international numbers held up. Reddit's response — testing a mandatory login requirement in international markets — may slow the data scraping, but it also raises the cost of discovery for new users who arrive precisely through anonymous search.

What makes this more than a single-company story is the structural implication. Reddit was supposed to be AI-proof: irreducibly human, messy, community-generated content that machines couldn't replicate. Instead, AI turns out not to need to replicate it — only to summarize it, for free, at the point of search. Every publisher that monetizes search traffic is watching the same clock.
stories.hook: The internet spent twenty years building content for Google; Google is spending this year building answers out of that content instead.

stories.title: The Fed Just Decided to Decide Less Often
stories.story:
On October 28, the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate steady at 3.75–4%, exactly as markets expected. But the rate decision was almost beside the point. The headline from Chairman Kevin Warsh's press conference was structural: the Fed is redesigning its own calendar. Starting in 2027, one of the eight annual FOMC meetings will carry no rate vote and no policy statement — reserved instead for what Warsh called thinking about "big questions." By 2028, two of eight meetings will operate that way, leaving only six formal decision points per year.

This is not a tweak. For decades, the Fed has moved steadily toward more communication, not less — more press conferences, more dot plots, more forward guidance. Warsh is deliberately reversing that current. He's argued that longer gaps between rate-setting meetings allow data to accumulate and reduce the noise of reactive policymaking. Critics counter that fewer scheduled decision points don't make the Fed more deliberate; they just make it less legible, potentially amplifying volatility when the remaining meetings arrive.

The timing carries its own irony. Inflation is running at 3.7%, two FOMC members dissented in favor of an immediate hike, and markets are already pricing an 85% probability of a December increase. This is precisely the environment in which markets crave more Fed communication, not less. The December meeting — now carrying the weight of a skipped October hike and Warsh's new philosophy — has become the most consequential single data point on the 2026 calendar. What Warsh is betting is that a central bank that speaks less can, paradoxically, be trusted more. That wager won't be tested until the next shock arrives faster than the meeting schedule allows.
stories.hook: The Fed spent thirty years learning to say more — Warsh just decided the experiment is over.
